question: Though the new agreement concerning the revision of the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) introduces an automatic safeguard clause for rice imports from developing countries, its activation conditions are so difficult to trigger that it does not provide any meaningful protection to the Italian and EU rice industries.

EU rice imports will only be subject to tariffs if they outstrip 561 000 tonnes in a given year, an unreasonably high figure which was calculated by taking the average amount that the EU has imported from the likes of Myanmar and Cambodia over the last ten years and increasing it by 45 %.

It is also a concern that a large proportion of rice from Asian countries is produced using banned plant protection products and child labour. A key sector at national level, Italian rice-growing accounts for around 50 % of Europe’s needs. Unfortunately, production is falling significantly as a result of tariff-free Asian imports, which also threaten EU food security. In view of the above: 1.
How will the Commission ensure reciprocity of standards for rice imported from Asian countries in a manner that takes the threat to consumer health into account?
Were imports to exceed the agreed threshold, how will the Commission go about triggering the aforementioned automatic clause in a timely manner?
What other complementary actions will the Commission take to support European rice production?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.2.2026) The co-legislators agreed on the political elements of the new Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) in December 20251.

The EU rice sector will have more tools to protect its interests in the GSP context, in recognition of its sensitivity and importance: (i) rice is defined as a sensitive product, without tariff preferences for all standard GSP and GSP+ beneficiaries; (ii) there are three safeguard mechanisms (general safeguards, special safeguards and special surveillance) which apply also to the rice sector; (iii) there will be a new, fully automatic safeguard mechanism, only for rice if the conditions are met.

The Commission will ensure this instrument is activated immediately, based on existing mechanisms for management of surveillance or quota. Beyond GSP, any food product imported in the EU must comply with the EU sanitary and phytosanitary requirements. This is not negotiable. Moreover, the EU Vision for Agriculture2 will strive toward fairer global level playing field for agriculture, including on pesticides.

The Commission also works to strengthen controls on imports and establish a principle that the most hazardous pesticides banned in the EU are not allowed for imported products. Additionally, for the next two years the Commission3 announced a 50% increase in the number of audits carried outside the EU. Also, the Unity Safety Net proposed in the next Multiannual Financial Framework (EUR 6.

3 billion over seven years, roughly doubling the current agricultural reserve) will help safeguard farmers from potential major market disruptions. Finally, under the EU promotion policy to boost the EU's agri-food competitiveness and its export market diversification, EUR 205 million is available to launch programmes and actions in 2026.
